title: The model that wins on cross-validation loses on a new machine: extrapolation, long-range saturation and physics constraints in confinement scaling
description:
An analysis of machine learning for tokamak energy confinement time on the real ITPA Global H-mode Confinement Database (HDB5, standard analysis set STD5). A random forest beats the published IPB98(y,2) scaling law by 41% in RMSLE under grouped cross-validation by discharge; under leave-one-tokamak-out the ordering of the fitted models reverses exactly, and the forest is worse than a log-linear power law on 13 of 13 held-out machines.

The failure is characterised three ways: error tracking the Mahalanobis distance of the held-out machine from the training data, the hard prediction bound of a tree ensemble, and a polynomial flexibility ladder showing that what flexibility costs is the tail of the error distribution rather than its centre. Ordering machines by size reproduces, inside the database, a size extrapolation matching the 1.82x jump from the database to ITER; at that cut the tree ensembles score closer to a constant predictor than to the power law.

A constrained hybrid (a power law plus a bounded, heavily damped correction on its log residuals) is then built and scored, and is the best blind model at the ITER-matched cut. Split-conformal intervals calibrated to 90% under cross-validation are shown to cover 35% of rows on an unseen machine and 3% across the ITER-matched cut, at essentially unchanged interval width.

Two repairs are then built and scored. A power law plus a bounded, heavily damped correction on its log residuals is the best blind model at the ITER-matched cut among the learned models. Imposing the Connor-Taylor constraints instead, which any scaling law expressible in dimensionless variables must satisfy, as linear equality constraints on the exponents beats it: 0.183 RMSLE at that cut, the best blind score in the study, with no hyperparameter. The constraint derivation is validated externally, in that IPB98(y,2) as published in 1999 lands on the Kadomtsev surface at a distance of 0.00096. Supplying the same physics as a shrinkage prior rather than a constraint is shown to be worth substantially less.

Calibrating conformal intervals on held-out machines rather than held-out discharges restores coverage to within two points of nominal on an unseen machine, and, as the exchangeability diagnosis predicts, fails to restore it across the size cut. The reversal is replicated on 5358 H-mode rows the standard analysis set does not contain and on 3860 ohmic and L-mode rows scored against ITER89-P, with the ranking inverting in both. A locked, digest-stamped prediction is recorded for SPARC, JT-60SA and ITER: inside the database's size range the models agree to within 15 percent, and at ITER they disagree by a factor of 8.3, with the tree ensembles arithmetically unable to reach the physics answer.

The audit is then run outside fusion twice. On 541 mammalian species records across 11 taxonomic orders, with Kleiber's published 3/4 exponent as the baseline, the extrapolation failure reproduces in full while the ranking reversal does not. On 3599 woody plants from the Biomass And Allometry Database, varying only the number of predictors on a fixed set of rows, the flexible models' interpolation margin crosses zero between two and three predictors while their deficit on a held-out species does not shrink, and the power law wins the held-out species at 4 of 4 feature counts. The extrapolation failure is therefore unconditional and the ranking reversal is not: the reversal requires the flexible model to win the interpolation split first, which makes it the warning sign rather than the hazard.

A final result corrects the study's own diagnosis. Separating flexibility from boundedness with a Gaussian process, whose behaviour far from the data is a choice of kernel rather than a tuning parameter, shows the failure belongs to boundedness. A bounded RBF kernel scores 1.948 at the ITER-matched cut, worse than predicting a constant; adding a linear term to the same kernel gives the best cross-validated score in the study, 0.112, together with 0.191 at the ITER-matched cut and 92.5 percent coverage of a nominal 90 percent interval that was never recalibrated. Models bounded by their training targets are the hazard, not flexible models.

Two arms test whether the headline is an artifact of the analyst's discretionary choices. Running the comparison under every combination of three of them, whether the wall-variant machines count as their own devices or as the tokamaks they are, whether error is pooled over rows or averaged over machines, and whether cross-validation is scored on all rows or only the machines leave-one-out can score, the inversion holds in all 8 cells. Exact sign tests give 13 of 13 machines by database label (p = 0.00024) and 11 of 11 by physical device (p = 0.00098). Separately, the distance correlation is checked against its own small-sample uncertainty by permutation and jackknife; the newer ITPA20 and ITPA20-IL scalings are scored as baselines alongside IPB98(y,2), which remains the strongest of the three on this database; and refitting the exponents by orthogonal distance regression, which places error on the predictors rather than only on the target, is reported as a sensitivity check rather than a corrected fit.

A domain-agnostic module packages the method for reuse on other scaling-law datasets: leave-one-group-out scoring reported alongside extrapolation distance and the training-range bound, an ordered-group splitter, and equality-constrained least squares as a scikit-learn estimator.

The repository contains the full pipeline, from-scratch least-squares solvers, all analysis scripts, the test suite, and the scripts that regenerate every reported number and figure. The HDB5 dataset itself is third-party data obtained from OSF and is not redistributed here; it is pinned by SHA-256 and verified on load.
